title: 'Abasa: he frowned
hookLine: the Prophet ﷺ turned from a blind man to talk to the powerful, and was corrected (80:1–10)
carry: turn to the one who came

lines: FINALLY TALKING TO THE RIGHT PERSON.
cards: A work event. You're finally talking to the one person in the room who could change everything: the investor, the boss's boss, the person with the answer. Then a tap on your shoulder.
The intern, or an old neighbor, asking a question that could wait. You don't say anything rude. Your face just does a small thing.
A flicker. A frown. It would be easy never to think about it again.
The surah just before At-Takwir is named after that flicker. And the surprise is whose face it was. Today: 'Abasa, he frowned.

teach.b: Surah eighty opens, in Pickthall's words: He frowned and turned away Because the blind man came unto him. Sunni commentators, following reports in Tirmidhi and the tafsir, explain the scene this way.
The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was in Mecca, speaking with leaders of the Quraysh, hoping they would listen.

teach.h: IBN UMM MAKTUM, WHO CAME TO LEARN.
teach.b: A blind man, 'Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum, came up asking to be taught. The Prophet frowned and turned back to the leaders, and revelation came correcting him.

Shia commentators such as al-Tabataba'i, and some others, read it differently: the one who frowned was another man present, not the Prophet. Both readings are held with care. Now listen to how the correction is spoken.
It begins in the third person, he frowned, which commentators read as courtesy, the text almost looking away.

Then it speaks directly: what could tell you, perhaps he would grow in purity, or be reminded, and the reminder would help him. As for the one who thinks he needs nothing, you give him your attention.
But the one who came to you eagerly, and in awe, him you neglect.

teach.h: A CORRECTION KEPT IN THE TEXT.
teach.b: And the correction stays in the text, recited ever since. What happened next?
Ibn Umm Maktum became a caller to prayer in Medina, alongside Bilal, and reports say the Prophet left him in charge of the prayer in Medina when he traveled.

teach.h: TURN TO THE ONE WHO CAME.
teach.b: The man turned away from became the voice calling the city to prayer.

how: Muslims cite 'Abasa as a lesson that sincerity outweighs status; Ibn Umm Maktum is remembered as a companion and muezzin, and the surah sits in Juz' 'Amma, the thirtieth part of the Qur'an, often learned by heart early.

o: he wept, moved by what he heard
he was angry, and spoke harshly
he frowned, the surah's first word

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: the blind man who came to learn
the one who thinks he needs nothing
a caller to prayer with Bilal

s: the Qur'an keeps a correction in its own text
'Abasa opens with it, and it has been recited ever since.
all commentators agree on who frowned
Sunni commentators say the Prophet; Shia commentators such as al-Tabataba'i say another man present.
Ibn Umm Maktum stayed on the edges of the community
he became a muezzin in Medina, and reports say he led the prayer there when the Prophet traveled.

games.q: you're talking with powerful people who might finally listen. a blind man interrupts, eager to learn. what does the surah say about him?
o: he should have waited his turn
perhaps he would grow in purity
games.why: perhaps he would grow in purity, or be reminded (80:3–4). the eager one was the one to turn to.

practice: Think of the people who come to you and are easy to overlook: the quiet coworker, the kid who wants to show you something, the older relative who repeats a story, the person at the counter.
Pick one, and picture the next time they come to you, and you turn fully toward them: phone down, eyes up, full attention.

wordCard.voice: 'Abasa. He frowned, the name of Surah eighty, which turns our attention to the one who came eagerly. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: "he frowned," the first word and the name of Surah 80.

carryVoice: Your line: turn to the one who came. The eager one was the one to turn to. That's day two hundred thirteen.

sources.q: He frowned and turned away Because the blind man came unto him.
